summary.text: For an arbitrary bound \(N\), apply the assumed decomposition to \((N+6)!/6=x+y\), so that \((N+6)!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\). If either the Sophie Germain primes or the lower members of twin pairs were bounded by \(N\), the corresponding bounded prime (or the twin pair’s upper prime) would divide the factorial and hence divide the other summand; primality forces the two summands to be equal, but then \(12x-1=3(4y+1)\), contradicting its primality.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs. Thus infinitude of \(\mathcal T\) is exactly infinitude of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is obtained by considering each integer \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), putting \(y=n-x\), and counting \(x\) if all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Notice that
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Likewise,
\[
(6y-1)+2=6y+1,
\]
so the last two conditions say that \(6y-1,6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume the conjectured positivity statement
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
Because \(a(n)\) is a sum of zero-one indicator terms, its positivity means that at least one term is equal to one. Consequently, for every \(n>1\), there are positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Indeed, the counted index satisfies \(1\le x<n\), and hence \(y=n-x\ge1\).

We will prove separately that \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) are unbounded. Any unbounded set of natural numbers is infinite, so this will prove both required conclusions.

First we prove that the Sophie Germain primes are unbounded. Let \(N\) be an arbitrary nonnegative integer. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is no Sophie Germain prime greater than \(N\); equivalently, every member of \(\mathcal S\) is at most \(N\).

Set
\[
M=N+6,\qquad F=M!,\qquad n=\frac{F}{6}.
\]
Since \(M\ge6\), the integer \(6\) divides \(F=M!\), so \(n\) is an integer and
\[
6n=F.
\]
Also \(F\ge 5!=120\), and hence \(n=F/6\ge20>1\). We may therefore apply the positivity hypothesis at this value of \(n\). It supplies positive integers \(x,y\) satisfying
\[
x+y=n
\]
and such that all four numbers
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad s=12x-1,\qquad r=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1
\]
are prime.

The two primes \(p\) and \(s\) satisfy
\[
s=2p+1,
\]
so \(p\in\mathcal S\). By the assumed bound on \(\mathcal S\),
\[
p\le N<M.
\]
Moreover, because \(x\ge1\), we have \(p=6x-1\ge5\). Every positive integer at most \(M\) divides \(M!\); hence
\[
p\mid F.
\]
On the other hand, multiplying \(x+y=n\) by \(6\) and using \(6n=F\) gives
\[
F=6x+6y=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+q.
\]
Since \(p\mid F\) and \(p\mid p\), this equality implies
\[
p\mid q.
\]
But \(q\) is prime. Every positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself, so there are two cases:

1. \(p=1\). This is impossible because \(p\ge5\).

2. \(p=q\). In this case
\[
6x-1=6y+1.
\]
Using this equality, we calculate
\[
12x-1=3(4y+1).
\]
Indeed, the displayed equality gives \(6x=6y+2\), and therefore \(12x-1=12y+3=3(4y+1)\). Since \(y\ge1\), one has \(4y+1\ge5\). Thus \(12x-1\) is divisible by \(3\) and is strictly greater than \(3\). It is therefore composite, contradicting the fact that \(s=12x-1\) is prime.

Both possible cases are contradictory. Hence our supposition that all Sophie Germain primes are at most \(N\) was false. Since \(N\) was arbitrary, for every \(N\) there is a Sophie Germain prime greater than \(N\). Thus \(\mathcal S\) is unbounded and consequently infinite.

We next prove that the twin-prime pairs are unbounded. Again let \(N\) be arbitrary, and suppose for a contradiction that no lower member of a twin-prime pair is greater than \(N\). Thus every element of \(\mathcal T\) is at most \(N\).

Use exactly the same factorial construction:
\[
M=N+6,\qquad F=M!,\qquad n=\frac{F}{6}.
\]
As above, \(6\mid F\), \(6n=F\), and \(n>1\). The positivity hypothesis therefore gives positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) for which
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad s=12x-1,\qquad r=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1
\]
are all prime.

Here \(q=r+2\), so \(r\in\mathcal T\). The assumed bound gives
\[
r=6y-1\le N.
\]
Consequently,
\[
q=6y+1=r+2\le N+2<N+6=M.
\]
Also \(y\ge1\), so \(q=6y+1\ge7\). Since \(q\) is a positive integer at most \(M\), it divides \(M!=F\):
\[
q\mid F.
\]
As before, the relation \(x+y=n\) yields
\[
F=6n=6x+6y=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+q.
\]
It follows from \(q\mid F\) and \(q\mid q\) that
\[
q\mid p.
\]
The number \(p=6x-1\) is prime, so a positive divisor \(q\) of \(p\) must be either \(1\) or \(p\). Again there are two cases:

1. \(q=1\). This is impossible because \(q\ge7\).

2. \(q=p\). Then
\[
6y+1=6x-1,
\]
and exactly as above this implies
\[
12x-1=3(4y+1).
\]
Because \(y\ge1\), the right-hand side is a multiple of \(3\) greater than \(3\). Hence \(12x-1\) is composite, contradicting its required primality.

Thus the lower members of twin-prime pairs cannot all be bounded by \(N\). Since \(N\) was arbitrary, \(\mathcal T\) is unbounded, and therefore infinite.

We have shown that the assumed positivity of \(A227923(n)\) for every \(n>1\) forces both the set of Sophie Germain primes and the set of twin-prime pairs to be infinite.
